To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cortical network for directed spatial attention is composed of four components that are anatomically distinct but functionally complementary: the posterior parietal lobe provides a sensory map of extrapersonally space, the cingulate provides a motivational map, the frontal eye fields provide a schema for the exploration of that space, and the basal forebrain reticular formation provides the level of arousal that allows directed attention to be focused in extrapersonal rather than intrapersonal space

the cortical networks for directed attention and visual neglect are composed of four distinct components, each with a unique functional role, that are interconnected in such a way that damage to one or more of these components can produce a wide range of partial or complete unilateral neglect syndromesin monkeys and humans.

unilateral neglect reflects a disturbance of spatially directed attention, that four regions in the cerebral cortex provide an integrated network that modulates attention within extraperal space, and that each of these components of the attentional network has a distinct role in the spatial distribution and control of attention.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the localization and functional organization of a network of cortical regions for directed attention.
the anatomical and functional architecture of the cerebral cortex, and in particular with the neural mechanisms underlying directed attention.
the localization and organization of the neural substrates of directed attention and the mechanisms by which they are integrated to yield a coherent representation of space.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cerebral cortex is not equipotential for spatially directed attention, but rather that the brain is a network of networks.
directed attention is a function of the cortical network for directed spatial attention, and that unilateral neglect is a disturbance of that network.
the brain is neither a set of discrete, specialized modules nor a single, uniform, undifferentiated mass.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
unilateral neglect is a disorder of the spatial distribution of attention, and that this disorder reflects a disturbance of a cortical network that is distributed across several cerebral regions.
unilateral neglect is the result of damage to a distributed cortical network for spatial attention.
the brain is not a homogeneous mass, but rather a mosaic of functionally distinct components, each with its own anatomical boundaries and unique functional role.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a cortical network approach is useful for understanding complex brain-behavior relationships, such as those involved in the spatial distribution and control of attention.
unilateral neglect is not a unitary phenomenon.
unilateral neglect is a complex disorder with many different manifestations, and it is not a single disorder but rather a family of related disorders that are all caused by damage to the brain.
